implementation_notes: A scala.collection.immutable.TreeMap keyed by LocalDate is the temporal collection: byStart.rangeTo(when).lastOption returns the latest version effective on that date, rangeFrom/rangeUntil give the history windows and a traversal gives milestones() without sorting, while java.time.LocalDate (with an explicit Ordering if needed) is the Time Point. The owner keeps salaryAt(when: LocalDate) and a no-argument salary(today) form, and case-class values keep every stored version immutable, with the whole collection replaced rather than mutated. What replaces the classic structure: the persistent sorted map's range API; explicit Effectivity ranges are still justified when validity is not a simple 'latest start <= date' - gaps, overlaps, or several values at once - or when the history must be stored relationally.
pitfalls: TreeMap.updated at an existing key replaces the version silently and the map has no notion of a range, so a same-date correction or a split interval needs an entry-level key or explicit ranges.

rangeTo requires an implicit Ordering for the key; LocalDate's default ordering is the proleptic ISO calendar, and mixing it with ZonedDateTime/Instant keys (or relying on the ambient zone when creating dates) silently shifts day boundaries.
LocalDate.now() uses the JVM default zone: inject a java.time.Clock so the default-time accessor and its tests are reproducible, and so a server in another zone cannot change settlement dates.

A persistent TreeMap copies only the path on update, but reading the history from a database means rebuilding it per query (O(n log n)) or tracking deltas - the immutability that makes the in-memory code pleasant is exactly what makes the persistence mapping explicit work.
